Header:
Date: 2025-04-15
Start: 10:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Marcus Li (Redwood SRE), Priya Raman (CSM); Aisha Khan (NovaMaps ML Lead), Tom Reyes (Platform), Evan Cho (VP Product), Linda Park (QA), Jared Moss (Dev)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Intermittent 5xx spikes aligned with short windows of burst traffic during client retries. Sharing logs + proposed circuit-breaker description.
Topics: reliability incident recap; retry/backoff behavior; rate limit tuning; KV/prefix cache TTL; batching and quantization tradeoffs; next steps for soak test and RCA.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: OK everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump straight into the reliability items from last week.
[00:12] Aisha: hey, thanks. We had three main incidents last week, roughly 10:45, 13:02 and 17:30 UTC where our integration started seeing 503s and timeouts. Our app retried aggressively which made it worse.
[00:25] Tom: The stack is basically client -> redwood hosted api -> dedicated pool for the POC, there's a short circuit we added on the client but it was still firing lots of retries.
[00:36] Lena: right, and from our side we saw the spikes correlate with sequence lengths — longer sequences amplified token costs and per-request CPU, causing queueing. Also some kv cache churn when different prompt prefixes came in. Note: K V cache in the logs shows high miss rate.
[00:48] Marcus: we also saw a small fleet of nodes report RPC backpressure. The TTFB increased and some requests hit the per-node rate limiter, causing 429 which client translated to retry loops and then 5xx when queues overflowed.
[01:05] Evan: so is the immediate culprit the client retry policy or something in the runtime?
[01:12] Samir: both. There's a feedback loop: retries -> burst -> queueing -> more 5xx. Hypothesis: client retries without jitter and very short backoff, plus our batching threshold at the time wasn't tuned for these bursts.
[01:26] Aisha: For context, our users do short chat-like queries but occasionally a few heavy transform jobs that produce long sequences. Those heavy jobs coincide with periodic batch jobs from our side.
[01:38] Jared: small note, our platform had a cron that launched 200 parallel requests at minute boundaries — that likely created the long tail. We changed it post-incident but logs still show residual problems.
[01:50] Lena: Thanks. On the runtime we tried to reproduce. Reproduced a 429->retry amplification locally by sending synthetic bursts; when client retries had no exponential backoff the cluster got into a spiral. Adding a simple exponential backoff with jitter in the client eliminated the spiral in tests.
[02:10] Tom: what about KV cache tuning? You mentioned TTLs — can you expand?
[02:17] Lena: Sure. Currently prefix caching TTLs are short (30s) because of prompt variability; result: high churn, frequent cold KV requests, extra compute. Increasing TTL for stabilized prefixes to 5 minutes reduces misses and average latency for repeated prompts. But risk: stale cache if prompts evolve.
[02:34] Linda: QA saw timeouts around 15s thresholds. Some requests floated for 18–22s before failing client-side.
[02:42] Marcus: We also observed retries causing queue depth to spike which then started returning internal 500s from the runtime when memory pressure hit. Those 5xxs are symptomatic, not root cause. Root is workload shaping + retry loops.
[02:58] Aisha: Any quick mitigations we can flip now?
[03:02] Samir: Immediate list: 1) Tighten client retry backoff + add jitter (your side). 2) Redwood to enable a temporary per-route concurrency cap and circuit-breaker to shed load instead of returning 500s. 3) Increase prefix cache TTL for common prompts. 4) Adjust batching window to favor smaller, faster batches during bursts.
[03:22] Tom: For the per-route cap, what numbers are you thinking?
[03:26] Marcus: For the POC pool we suggest capping at 60 concurrent in-flight requests per route as a start; we can lower to 40 if still unstable.
[03:34] Evan: will that increase latency?
[03:37] Lena: Possibly for peak requests, but it's better than large variance and 5xxs. We can also route non-critical jobs to a lower-cost queue.
[03:47] Jared: We want to avoid dropping user requests silently; is there a graceful fallback?
[03:50] Samir: yes the SDK supports a 503+Retry-After with metadata; also recommend graceful degrade to cached answer or shorter model.
[03:59] Linda: QA asked whether the retries visible in our logs include the SDK-level automatic retries or our app's custom ones.
[04:05] Tom: mostly our app-level retries, we didn't turn on SDK auto-retry.
[04:09] Lena: good to know. SDK auto-retry uses exponential backoff by default so it's safer.
[04:15] Aisha: About the 5xx patterns, can you share the node-level logs? There were traces that show OOMs around some requests.
[04:22] Marcus: We saw transient OOMs when KV cache misses caused larger allocations. We're instrumenting memory utilization per model instance; I'll pull the graphs and share.
[04:31] Samir: we'll upload three artifacts: incident timeline, raw request/response samples (anonymized), and node metrics. Expect those by EOD Thursday.
[04:40] Evan: on longer term, we'd like recommendations on batching and quantization tradeoffs; we noticed cost jumped with the more conservative quant profile.
[04:48] Lena: Quantization lowered memory but the kernel selection sometimes increased latency for some sequence lengths — it's a tradeoff. We'll produce a tuned config that tries int8 where it's beneficial and falls back for long sequences.
[04:58] Tom: About the per-route rate-limiting, will that be visible in our logs as 429s or will you return 503 so client can fallback?
[05:05] Marcus: we can surface 429 with Retry-After. It's cleaner than opaque 500s.
[05:10] Aisha: Great. Are you recommending client changes only or server side too?
[05:14] Samir: both. Short-term: client backoff + server per-route cap + circuit-breaker. Medium: KV TTL adjustments + batching window tuning. Long-term: workload-aware routing and smarter autoscaling policies.
[05:26] Linda: QA will run a set of jittered load tests once we get the new client config. We'll coordinate.
[05:32] Jared: Do we have a way to replay the exact POC load pattern? The cron that hit at minute boundaries is gone but we want to re-run with jitter.
[05:40] Marcus: we'll share the reproduction script and a framework to replay. It includes the same distribution of short vs long sequences.
[05:47] Aisha: timeline then?
[05:49] Samir: Action items are in the notes. We'll reconvene in one week for a soak report. If the stabilized config shows improvement we'll plan a canary to more traffic.
[05:58] Tom: one more quick question — do you have a recommended client-side token limit to prevent runaway long sequences?
[06:04] Lena: set a soft cap at 2k tokens for now and force-truncate beyond that with a user warning. Also consider streaming for long outputs.
[06:14] Evan: ok thanks. Anything else?
[06:17] Priya: just to confirm, you'll share the incident artifacts and Marcus will flip the circuit-breaker; NovaMaps will run the soak and report back?
[06:26] Aisha: yes.
[06:28] Samir: Great. We'll close there — thanks everyone.
